name: False Consensus Effect
description: People overestimate how many other people share their own beliefs, choices, or habits. Our own view feels more normal and representative than it really is.
design_relevance_note: Directly relevant to product discovery, stakeholder alignment, and research interpretation: teams can assume their own preferences are widespread among users, while participants can also misreport how common their own behavior is when asked about 'people like them.'
prevalence_note: A classic social-judgment bias with obvious product-research relevance, and a common caution in UX circles against assuming the team or heavy users are representative of everyone else.

findings.description: A meta-analysis found social projection (expecting others to be similar to oneself) is substantially stronger for ingroups than outgroups, with outgroup projection positive but small. Ingroup projection is stronger for laboratory-created groups than real social categories; analysis mode and judgment order showed no discernible effects. Supports social projection functioning as an egocentric heuristic for inductive reasoning, contributing to ingroup favoritism and perceived ingroup homogeneity.
findings.source_title: Social Projection to Ingroups and Outgroups: A Review and Meta-Analysis

findings.description: Across choice and trait-judgment tasks, participants overestimated how many other people would share their own choice, belief, or behavior, and they judged dissenters as more abnormal than warranted — direct evidence for the false consensus effect as an egocentric social-perception bias.
findings.source_title: The “false consensus effect”: An egocentric bias in social perception and attribution processes

applications.title: How mainstream media's false consensus contributed to the 2016 election surprise
applications.description: In the lead-up to the 2016 US presidential election, most mainstream media outlets, political pundits, and pollsters predicted a decisive Hillary Clinton victory. Analysis attributes part of this miscalculation to the false consensus effect: because media and political elites personally found Donald Trump's rhetoric unpalatable, they assumed the broader public shared that reaction, leading to a systematic underestimation of his actual support.
applications.ethical_note: This documents a real, consequential instance of the false consensus effect in political forecasting, not a persuasion or product-design case -- there is no UI or business decision being evaluated, only journalists and forecasters mistaking their own reaction for a population-wide one.
